routes.label: Wilmington to Philadelphia (Thomas Garrett)
routes.source: Foner, "Middle Atlantic", NPS Underground Railroad Handbook (Dickinson, HB-FONER); Wikipedia, "Thomas Garrett" (WP-GARRETT)
routes.note: TEST ROW for the Underground Railroad layer (owner's request of 2026-11-17); not reviewed. Research and full citations: docs/UNDERGROUND-RAILROAD.md. Garrett worked in Wilmington from 1822 and sent people on to the Philadelphia committee. 1861: J. Miller McKim's remark that the Underground Railroad was in effect over (HB-FONER); the NPS itself runs it to 1865. Places, in order: Wilmington, Philadelphia.

routes.label: Across the Ohio at Ripley
routes.note: TEST ROW for the Underground Railroad layer (owner's request of 2026-11-17); not reviewed. Research and full citations: docs/UNDERGROUND-RAILROAD.md. Ripley (John Rankin from 1822, John Parker) to Sardinia. The story of Rankin's lantern appears only in twentieth-century sources. Places, in order: Ripley, Sardinia.

routes.label: Sardinia to Lake Erie
routes.note: TEST ROW for the Underground Railroad layer (owner's request of 2026-11-17); not reviewed. Research and full citations: docs/UNDERGROUND-RAILROAD.md. Northwest to join the Cincinnati road in the upper Miami valley, then by the Alum Creek Quaker settlement north of Columbus to Sandusky. The source dates these networks to "the late 1820s and early 1830s" and names a belt of settlements, not a list of towns: Urbana stands for the belt. Places, in order: Sardinia, Urbana, Sandusky.

routes.label: Cincinnati to Lake Erie
routes.note: TEST ROW for the Underground Railroad layer (owner's request of 2026-11-17); not reviewed. Research and full citations: docs/UNDERGROUND-RAILROAD.md. By farmers' wagons through the Quaker and free Black settlements between Lebanon and Urbana, then by Alum Creek to Sandusky and the Western Reserve. In use from about 1830, dense by about 1840; Levi Coffin moved to Cincinnati in 1847. Places, in order: Cincinnati, Lebanon, Urbana, Sandusky.

routes.label: Across the Ohio at Madison
routes.note: TEST ROW for the Underground Railroad layer (owner's request of 2026-11-17); not reviewed. Research and full citations: docs/UNDERGROUND-RAILROAD.md. Madison (George DeBaptiste, Elijah Anderson) to Levi Coffin at Newport, now Fountain City, where he lived from 1826 to 1847. The source gives the way between by county only. Places, in order: Madison, Newport (Fountain City).

routes.label: Across the Ohio at New Albany
routes.note: TEST ROW for the Underground Railroad layer (owner's request of 2026-11-17); not reviewed. Research and full citations: docs/UNDERGROUND-RAILROAD.md. New Albany and Jeffersonville, Canton, Farmington, Azalia, Carthage, Newport: the stops are the source's. The years are Coffin's at Newport; the source does not date this road itself. Places, in order: New Albany, Canton, Azalia, Carthage, Newport (Fountain City).

routes.label: Cincinnati to Newport
routes.note: TEST ROW for the Underground Railroad layer (owner's request of 2026-11-17); not reviewed. Research and full citations: docs/UNDERGROUND-RAILROAD.md. Three roads met at Coffin's house: from Madison, from New Albany and from Cincinnati. Places, in order: Cincinnati, Newport (Fountain City).

routes.label: Newport to Michigan
routes.note: TEST ROW for the Underground Railroad layer (owner's request of 2026-11-17); not reviewed. Research and full citations: docs/UNDERGROUND-RAILROAD.md. From Newport to Detroit, or to the free Black settlements of Cass County, Michigan (Cassopolis is its county seat and stands for them). Places, in order: Newport (Fountain City), Cassopolis, Detroit.

routes.label: Louisiana to Mexican Texas
routes.source: Baumgartner, "Freedom Seekers on the Southwestern Frontier", NPS handbook (HB-BAUM); Wikipedia, "Underground Railroad" (WP-UGRR)
routes.note: TEST ROW for the Underground Railroad layer (owner's request of 2026-11-17); not reviewed. Research and full citations: docs/UNDERGROUND-RAILROAD.md. A direction, not a road. Nearly a hundred people left western Louisiana in the summer of 1822, across the Sabine (then the border) for Nacogdoches and San Antonio de Béxar. Natchitoches as the line's start is the editor's choice (WP-UGRR mentions a road from there); the escapes the source dates were from parishes farther south. Ends in 1836, when Texas left Mexico. Places, in order: Natchitoches, Nacogdoches, San Antonio.

routes.label: Carolina to Spanish Florida
routes.source: NPS, "Fort Mose" (NPS-MOSE); Florida Museum, "Fort Mose" (FLMNH); Wikipedia, "Fort Mose" (WP-MOSE)
routes.note: TEST ROW for the Underground Railroad layer (owner's request of 2026-11-17); not reviewed. Research and full citations: docs/UNDERGROUND-RAILROAD.md. A direction, not a road: no source names a place between Carolina and St. Augustine. First arrivals by canoe in 1687 (Landers, by a search result only; Wikipedia has 1689); Charles II's edict of 1693; Fort Mose founded 1738, evacuated to Cuba in 1763. Charleston stands for Carolina. Places, in order: Charleston, Fort Mose.

routes.label: Cape Florida to the Bahamas
routes.source: Wikipedia, "Saltwater Railroad" (WP-SALT); Baram, "Trail toward liberty", Journal of Florida Studies (BARAM)
routes.note: TEST ROW for the Underground Railroad layer (owner's request of 2026-11-17); not reviewed. Research and full citations: docs/UNDERGROUND-RAILROAD.md. From Cape Florida on Key Biscayne across the Gulf Stream to Andros Island (the Red Bays settlement): about 300 Black Seminoles in the early 1820s. The crossing is documented; where on Andros they landed is not in what was read. Sources disagree on how long it ran (to the mid-1820s; "1821-1837"). Places, in order: Cape Florida (Key Biscayne), Andros Island.
